name: bochs
desc: Open source IA-32 (x86) PC emulator written in C++
why: An x86 PC emulator with a built-in debugger, letting you watch BIOS and boot code execute instruction by instruction.

brief.what_it_is: Bochs is an open source IA-32 (x86) PC emulator written in C++ that runs on most popular platforms. It emulates the Intel x86 CPU, common I/O devices, memory, and a custom BIOS, so you can run operating systems such as Linux, DOS, or Microsoft Windows inside a window on your own machine. The homepage describes it as a machine inside a machine, for example running Win95 applications on a Unix/X11 workstation. The pages I read do not describe a specific input format or output beyond the emulated display.
brief.why_it_exists: The README contrasts Bochs with virtualization products like VirtualBox and VMware: Bochs is an emulator, not virtualization, and it trades speed for a controlled, accurate execution environment. It is aimed at developing operating systems or bootloaders, handling very old mission-critical software, and reverse-engineering system-level code.
brief.how_it_works: Bochs emulates every CPU instruction in software rather than running guest code directly on the host CPU, which is why it is portable across architectures (the README mentions x86, ARM, and MIPS) and deterministic. It can be built to emulate many different x86 CPUs, from early 386 to recent x86-64 Intel and AMD processors. The pages I read do not explain the internal mechanism in more detail.
brief.install_notes: The homepage and GitHub README both say downloads are available from the SourceForge project page and the GitHub repository, and that the source tree is hosted on GitHub. The README points to the user guide and developer guide for usage and contributing, but I did not fetch those docs, so I have no configuration or first-run steps. Nothing I read mentions hardware, accounts, or runtimes.
brief.standout: Bochs is a full-system emulator that models the whole PC, including the CPU, devices, and a custom BIOS, and it stresses accuracy over speed. The scout note says it has a built-in debugger for stepping through BIOS and boot code one instruction at a time, but neither page I read mentions a debugger, so that claim is unverified from these sources.
brief.status: Maintained. The homepage says Bochs 3.1 was released on August 23, 2026, and the page was last modified on 23-Aug-2026. The GitHub README still names version 3.0 in its install section, which suggests it lags the homepage slightly. The homepage news list shows steady releases from 2011 to 2026, and the project asks for help with device models and disk images.
brief.caveats: The project says its bug tracker is full of issues from incomplete C++ models of PC devices, including mouse, interrupt controller, timer, IDE, network card, keyboard, and VGA. The project also says its disk image collection is out of date. Emulating every instruction makes it slower than virtualization products. The homepage describes the source as moving from SVN to GitHub, and the GitHub README still points to SourceForge for downloads. I did not check licensing or platform support details.

entry.title: Bochs
entry.tldr: Bochs is a software emulator of an entire x86 PC, CPU, devices and BIOS included, built for accuracy over speed.
entry.deeper_look:
Bochs emulates an Intel x86 PC in C++. It models the CPU, memory, common I/O devices and a custom BIOS, so an operating system such as Linux, DOS or Windows can boot inside a window on your machine. It can be built to emulate CPUs from the early 386 up to recent x86-64 Intel and AMD parts.

The key distinction is that Bochs is an emulator, not virtualization. Products like VirtualBox and VMware run guest code directly on the host CPU. Bochs interprets every instruction in software. In the project's words: "Bochs' emulation provides a controlled, accurate execution environment, at the cost of speed/performance." The README says this makes it portable across host architectures (x86, ARM and MIPS are mentioned).

The README says it is aimed at developing operating systems and bootloaders, running very old mission-critical software, and reverse-engineering system-level code. Because the whole machine is a program you can inspect, a PC stops being a black box. The scout notes a built-in debugger for stepping through BIOS and boot code, but the pages read for this entry do not mention one, so check the user guide before counting on it.

The install also gives you `bximage`, which is presumably the tool for making disk images. The sources read do not describe it, so look at its `--help`.

entry.whats_unique: It interprets every instruction of a whole PC in software, so it is deterministic and portable across host architectures, unlike the virtualization products it is often compared to.
entry.caveats: It is slower than virtualization, the project says its bug tracker holds issues from incomplete device models (VGA, IDE, network card and others), and its disk image collection is out of date.
